My cheap and relatively healthy bachelor chow:

Equipment:

Rice cooker ($20)

Measuring cups (set <$5)

Ingredients:

1/2 cup Rice, any kind works, I like jasmine. ($30/20lbs)

2 Eggs ($3/dozen)

1/2 cup Mixed frozen veggies ($4-6/lb)

2 tbsp Teriyaki or other flavored sauce ($3/bottle)

1 cup water

Combine water, rice and frozen vegetables in rice cooker, crack in eggs and set to white rice setting. Takes approx 25 minutes, serves 1. Cost is in the neighborhood of $.75/meal. It's easy to add more or less veggies and eggs to suit your taste, and if it isn't filling enough, double the water and rice without a significant price increase.

Instead of a recipe I want to give you a few tips.
1. Plan ahead. Check that you have everything your recipe calls for and that includes all the spices. Check which part of the dish requires the most time to cook and least amount of needed attention and do that part first (Not always the right call but for most simple recipes it is. That way your meal will be done faster and and when you serve it everything will be fresh.
2. Clean as you cook. The worst part of cooking is washing dishes but if you do it while waiting for pasta to cook it will make the time go faster and you will be happy at the end knowing you can just enjoy your meal.
3. Experiment with spices but be careful. Add enough for a subtle taste because you don't want everything to taste like pepper.
4. Don't snack while cooking. Tasting is fine but make it minimal. Tease yourself and you will enjoy the meal much more.
5. Experiment first by making scrambled eggs. Not just boring eggs, add bits of meat like bacon or ham, bits of veggies and whatever else you think would taste good. I really recommend adding a spoonfull of sour cream. Eggs are cheap, easy and super quick to make and almost everyone has their favorite way of making them. It's a great practice meal.
6. Recipes are guidelines. Don't worry about a missing ingredient because you can replace it with something else. You can add your own ingredient.
7. Know that sometimes you will fuck up. Learn from your mistakes.
8. When frying most things on a pan you should avoid putting the heat on high. High will quickly cook the outside but your meat may stay raw inside.
9. Rice is cheap and filling and great with almost anything but don't make too much because old cold rice is just not good.
10. Chicken breasts are very easy to cook. Cook it until it isn't pink at all and is just mostly white. It is incredibly easy to make it dry though so try to avoid that.
11. Make your favorite dish and improve it.
12. Have fun. Cooking is incredibly fun, satisfying and necessary for dating.

When I went to college my mom taught me this one recipe. It's super easy and very versatile.

You're going to need:

A base - rice or pasta work well

Meat (optional) - can be anything from cheap wieners to chicken to beef to minced pork, whatever

Vegetables - onions are a must, garlic wouldn't hurt, beans, corn, peas, bell peppers, chili peppers, carrots, olives, mushrooms, whatever you can get your hands on basically

Sauce of some sort - sour cream and tomato paste work well, you can spice it up by adding something fancier. I often used diced/crushed tomatoes (with the juice)

How to:

I don't want to get too complicated explaining this so lets say you chose rice, chicken, onion, garlic, a frozen bag of carrot-peas-corn mix, a red bell pepper, beans and tomato paste.

So you start by cooking the rice. While that's going on prepare the chicken by cutting it into thing slices. Chop onions and mince/cut garlic. You can also cut the bell pepper however you like (I prefer cutting it to slices and then into 2-3 parts to get small rectangles)

Now you're going to need a pan/pot big enough to hold all the ingredients (or just use less ingredients). Pour some oil (or melt some butter if you prefer) in the pot, add chicken and fry until it's almost cooked. Add onions and garlic and fry until onions become translucent.

So now that your meat and onion/garlic base is ready it's time to add everything else. A good way to start is to add the sauce first, that way you can season it easily. So add your tomato paste and stir. It's recommended to add a little bit of sugar to tomato sauces to remove the acidic taste, so you can throw some in. Stir and taste. Add salt, maybe basil, paprika wouldn't hurt. It takes some practice to get familiar with spices but even if you start out with just salt it's going to be fine.

After you've added the sauce add the vegetables (I recommend not adding the bell peppers quite yet, I prefer adding those in last so they retain some of their crunchiness), stir and let cook for a short while. Then add the rice, stir thoroughly, reduce heat to medium-low-ish and let simmer for a while.

And that's pretty much the basics. The rest is up to you, experiment with different combinations, play around with spices and sauces. Want something creamier? Throw in some cream cheese or even regular cheese.

Here's some tips:

If you have a lot of vegetables that need cutting, take some time off before hand, that way it'll be less hectic during the cooking process

If you have the time google things like "how to cut insert vegetable" so you can learn the easy way to prepare the things you're putting in your food

The longer you let it simmer the tastier it'll get, but technically it'll be ready pretty much 5-10 minutes after you add the last ingredients

Play around with proportions. If it's too dry, add more sauce. You can add more vegetables or make it more about the meat or your base. Whatever works for you, there's pretty much no wrong steps in this recipe.

Want to spice up the sauce? Add some mustard or garlic sauce. This is also why it's a good idea to add the sauce after the meat and onions are done, you can mix it up easily and taste to see if it fits.

Have fun!

Edit: the price range depends on what you use. I've made this recipe with $5 using cheap pasta, tomato sauce, some generic frozen vegetable mix and cheap wieners. Sometimes I've spent over $20 using more expensive sauces, fancier vegetables and better quality meat. As I said, very versatile.

A comparison of our view of Pluto two months ago and today.

One of my favorite things about New Horizons is that were seeing a (dwarf) planet for pretty much the first time.

The image of Pluto on the left was taken by the Hubble Space Telescope and that was the best picture of Pluto that we had up until not even two months ago when New Horizons imaging resolution exceeded the Hubble's on May 15, 2015. The image on the right is the latest image from New Horizons.
Question: Are there any questions we're hoping to get answered with these higher definition images we're getting back?
Question: Are there any questions we're hoping to get answered with these higher definition images we're getting back?

This is our first real glimpse at Pluto and Charon so the higher-definition images will allow us to map Pluto and Charon. New Horizons is doing much more than just taking pictures though. It has 3 primary objectives on its Pluto-Charon encounter...

  1. Characterize the global geography and morphology of Pluto and Charon
  2. Map chemical compositions of Pluto and Charon surfaces
  3. Characterize the neutral atmosphere of Pluto and its escape rate

However, these are the required objectives of the encounter and their are a number of secondary(expected) and tertiary(desired) objectives.

You can check out all the different objectives on the New Horizons Wikipedia page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Horizons#Objectives

Why is there a difference in image quality? More light? Closer image?

Closer image. The one on the left was taken using the Hubble Space Telescope, which is in orbit around Earth and the one on the right was using New Horizon's LORRI(Long-Range Reconnaissance Imager).

On May 15, 2015 New Horizons reached a close enough distance to Pluto that its imaging resolution exceeded the capabilities of Hubble and so each time New Horizons takes a new image as it gets closer and closer to Pluto each image has a little bit more detail than the last.
How is it that Hubble can take such stunning images of of galaxies and star clusters, but can't get good resolution on Pluto, which is much much closer. Is it the relative size of the objects?

I'm not an expert by any stretch of the imagination, but I think in terms of actual resolution of a galaxy if you compare the size of a galaxy to Pluto then the resolution would be much much lower for the galaxy. A single pixel of a high res photo of a galaxy would contain many star systems and you would not even get one pixel resolution of an object the size of Pluto from it.
Because Hubble was designed to look at galaxies light years away. Imagine trying to look at you hand using a set of binoculars. Your hand cant be focused upon because it just to close to the lens.

Think about how much light Pluto reflects compared to the light produced by a star and galaxies. Pluto is like a baseball on the other side of a football field and the star is akin to seeing a lighthouse miles out from the shore.
